title: Graceful degradation and capacity ladders for tenant-aware routing
content:
Purpose:

This note captures an operational pattern we should adopt for tenant-aware routing: a capacity ladder + graceful degradation framework enforced by the control plane and executed at regional proxies. The goal is to make SLAs enforceable, predictable, and resilient to noisy neighbors and region outages while minimizing customer-visible errors. This is a working doc — contains heuristics, trade-offs, and a suggested implementation plan.

Background / Motivation:

We currently route requests by tenant id + model selector and apply a mixture of global and per-region quotas. Observed failures during peak events show three common modes: (1) tenants exceeding burst capacity push other tenants into higher tail latency; (2) regional capacity pressure causes synchronous errors for many tenants rather than graceful fallbacks; (3) contractual expectations (SLA tiers) are not consistently honored when redistributing load across regions. We need a principled, operationally simple pattern to minimize these failures.

Core concepts and short definitions:

- Capacity ladder: an ordered set of capacity bands that a tenant may occupy. Bands map to routing policies, QoS settings, and allowed model variants. Example bands: reserved, committed, shared-normal, shared-degraded, degraded-cache-only.
- Graceful degradation: stepwise reduction in service fidelity (e.g., shorter max tokens, lower-cost model variant, cached-prefix-only responses) rather than immediate hard rejections.
- Control-plane policy: authoritative, centrally-managed rules describing band assignment, promotion/demotion triggers, and regional fallback priorities.
- Execution-plane enforcement: light-weight evaluation at the regional ingress/proxy that applies decisions within a short time window (10–60s) and emits telemetry back to control plane.

Principles and trade-offs:

1) Deterministic, time-bounded decisions: avoid per-request heavyweight policy evaluation. Control plane publishes band assignments and simple token-bucket/quota parameters; proxies apply them locally.

2) Prefer availability over fidelity where contracts permit: for lower SLA tiers, expose degraded-but-available responses (shorter generations, cache-only) rather than 429/5xx. Enterprise customers with higher SLAs get reserved lanes and strong fallbacks.

3) Explicit mapping of SLA to fallback chain: every SLA tier has a ranked list of fallback actions (region fallback, model variant fallback, degrade response size, cache-only). This mapping must be auditable and surfaced in billing/console.

4) Signals for demotion/promotion should be noisy-neighbor resistant: use aggregated, smoothed metrics (p50/p95 CPU or token-rate per-tenant, request-fanout, KV cache hit rates) and require multi-window confirmation before moving bands.

Architectural components and data flows:

- Control Plane (CP): maintains tenant profiles (tier, reserved capacity, fallback-chain, region preferences) and publishes signed band manifests every minute. CP also runs global allocators to produce reservation and borrow schedules during planned maintenance or predicted load spikes.

- Regional Proxy / Edge Enforcer (RE): consumes manifests, maintains local token-buckets and per-tenant state, executes fast policy (O(1) checks) and emits telemetry. RE also supports ephemeral priority boosts (short-lived tokens) to enable customer-initiated burst capacity.

- Router/Dispatcher: maps incoming requests to the proper RE or to cross-region fallback queues. It is responsible for attempting region-prefers first and failing over according to the tenant's fallback-chain when necessary.

- Telemetry & Decision Loop: RE emits aggregated tenant signals into CP; CP runs a demotion/promotion decision loop (30–120s windows) and publishes updated manifests. Manual overrides and incident playbooks are supported.

Band definitions and example policies:

Reserved: backed by Dedicated capacity. Zero best-effort evictions inside region unless operator triggers emergency maintenance. No model fidelity changes.

Committed: guaranteed throughput within a token bucket; overage flows to burst queue which has time-limited priority. Fallback chain: cross-region fallback -> model-variant fallback -> adaptive-token-throttle.

Shared-normal: normal shared pool. Prefers lowest-latency region per routing table. Fallback chain: model-variant fallback -> degrade-length -> cache-serve.

Shared-degraded: forced to cheaper model variants, reduced max tokens, and limited concurrency. Expect increased infer latency but lower compute per request.

Cache-only: only return responses when prefix/KV cache hit exists, otherwise return a structured fallback response (e.g., cached summary or 202 + async retry token) so clients can surface intermediate UX.

Noisy neighbor detection and controls:

- Detection signals: sustained per-tenant token-rate >> historical baseline, high per-tenant p99 latency for co-located tenants, sudden KV cache miss surge indicating working set change.
- Short-term mitigations: temporary per-tenant concurrency cap (seconds), ephemeral lease evaporation (borrowed tokens reclaimed), rate-limited tail shedding (prefer to shorten responses rather than reject).
- Mid-term responses: escalate to demotion band after confirmation windows; apply per-tenant backpressure headers visible to client SDKs.

Multi-region considerations and contract mapping:

- Region affinity: tenants can indicate preferred regions; allocation respects residency constraints for Private customers.
- Contract-aware failover: for tenants with explicit cross-region SLAs, CP will maintain a reservation in at least one secondary region (cold-standby capacity) and mark fallback-order explicitly.
- Split-brain avoidance: manifests include monotonic version + CP-signed validity TTL; RE refuses older manifests and hosts a local emergency policy that favors availability over strict quota adherence when CP is unreachable for >2m (with operator alarm).

Operational playbooks (runbooks):

- Spike detected (RE telemetry: sudden per-tenant token surge): RE applies short-term concurrency cap and emits incident event; CP evaluates over 30s window; if confirmed, CP moves tenant to next demotion band and notifies SE/customer success for high-tier tenants.

- Region outage: Router attempts secondary region per tenant fallback-chain. CP pushes emergency manifests with cross-region borrow allowances. If cross-region not allowed, Router returns graceful degradation responses per band mapping.

- Noisy neighbor: if noisy-behavior persists after two confirmation windows, apply mid-term demotion and bill mitigation actions (billing note + customer notification). For top-tier customers, schedule immediate operator review instead of demotion.

Metrics and SLAs to monitor:

- Per-tenant success rate by band (availability), median and p99 tail latency, cost-per-token delta when falling back to variant models, cache-hit ratio, number of cross-region fallbacks, frequency of band changes per tenant (should be low).

Implementation plan (phases):

1) Policy schema and manifest format (v1): CP defines JSON manifest (versioned, TTL, signed) containing tenant -> band, token-bucket params, fallback-chain. Minimal fields only to keep RE evaluation O(1).
2) RE enforcement shim: small footprint in edge proxy to apply buckets + fallback actions. Ship to a single region for testing with limited tenants.
3) Telemetry wiring and decision loop: CP reads RE aggregates and runs demotion/promotion rule engine with smoothing windows.
4) Fallbacks and model-variant plumbing: wire model catalog to routing so RE/Router can select cheaper variants when required.
5) Pilot with mix of tiers and a simulated noisy neighbor load (load test + chaos).

Open questions / trade-offs to decide:

- How aggressive should automatic demotion be for mid-tier tenants vs manual operator control?
- Exact smoothing window lengths (30s vs 120s) — shorter windows favor responsiveness; longer windows favor stability.
- Billing and transparency: include automated notifications and console visibility for every band-change to avoid surprises.

Next steps:

- Review with SRE and Solutions Eng to align on playbooks for top-tier customers (w/ manual override).
- Draft minimal manifest schema and RE shim API (API doc + example).

Notes-to-self: include example manifest snippet and RE pseudo-code in next revision.
